## Product Gallery App Structure Summary

### Framework
**Next.js 16** (Next.js 16.2.1-canary.21) with React 19.1.0, TypeScript

---

### 1. Main App Entry Point & Routing Setup

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `/vercel/sandbox/app/layout.tsx` | Root layout with metadata (title: "Product Gallery") |
| `/vercel/sandbox/app/page.tsx` | Home page route (`/`) - renders ProductGrid inside Suspense |
| `/vercel/sandbox/app/product/[slug]/page.tsx` | Dynamic product detail route (`/product/[slug]`) |

---

### 2. Product Grid Component

| File | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `/vercel/sandbox/app/ProductGrid.tsx` | Server component that maps over `products` array, renders Link cards with product image (colored div), name, and price |
| `/vercel/sandbox/app/ProductSkeleton.tsx` | Loading skeleton with pulsing animation for grid items |

---

### 3. Product Detail Page/Component

| File | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `/vercel/sandbox/app/product/[slug]/page.tsx` | Async server component with `Suspense` fallback. Shows product hero image, name, price, description. Includes back link. |
| `/vercel/sandbox/lib/products.ts` | Product data with 4 sample products (sneakers, backpack, headphones, hoodie) and `getProduct()` helper |

---

### 4. Animation/Transition Code

**Existing animations:** CSS-only pulse animation for skeleton loading states

| File | Animation |
|------|-----------|
| `/vercel/sandbox/app/globals.css` | `@keyframes pulse` (opacity 1 to 0.5) applied to `.skeleton-image` and `.skeleton-text` |

**No existing:** Framer Motion, GSAP, or CSS transitions/transforms for page transitions or product card hover effects.

---

### 5. CSS Styling

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `/vercel/sandbox/app/globals.css` | Global styles including `.product-grid` (CSS Grid), `.product-card`, `.product-detail` (2-column layout), skeleton animations |

---

### File Structure Overview

```
/vercel/sandbox/
├── app/
│   ├── layout.tsx           # Root layout
│   ├── page.tsx             # Home page (/)
│   ├── ProductGrid.tsx      # Product grid component
│   ├── ProductSkeleton.tsx  # Grid loading skeleton
│   ├── globals.css          # Global styles + animations
│   └── product/
│       └── [slug]/
│           └── page.tsx     # Product detail page (/product/[slug])
├── lib/
│   └── products.ts          # Product data + types
├── package.json             # Next.js 16 + React 19
└── ...config files
```

### Key Observations
- **No animation library** (framer-motion, GSAP) installed
- **CSS transitions/transforms** could be added for hover effects on product cards
- **Page transitions** are not implemented (Next.js Link navigation is instant)
- The skeleton loading uses a simple **CSS keyframe pulse animation**
</task_result>

---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

## Example

As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_.

We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions).

---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

## Example

As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_.

We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions).
